Photograph: Juan Mabromata/AFP/Getty Images Argentina President Javier Milei says ‘winds of change’ support Argentina’s claim to Falkland Islands President cites Donald Trump’s suggestion that he might reconsider US support for British sovereignty, and threatens swifter sanctions on British oil interests Tiago Rogero South America correspondent Fri 4 Sep 2026 05.31 EDT First published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 01.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google President Javier Milei has said “winds of change favourable” to Argentina’s claim to the Falkland Islands were “blowing around the world” in a televised address, citing signs that Donald Trump may reconsider the US position on the islands’ sovereignty. “Recently, President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas,” he said, using the Argentinian name for the islands. The Argentinian president said the UK was facing “multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. It is clear that they are on a path of decline. Argentina’s future, however, is flourishing and will prevail.” Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland Islands Read more Earlier on Thursday, Trump was asked by the British outlet GB News if he would “come to the UK’s aid” during a potential territorial dispute over the Falkland Islands with Argentina, and hinted that he would not, adding that the UK “weren’t there to help me [with Iran]”. Supporters had expected Milei to use his address to the nation on Thursday night to announce an unprecedented US endorsement of Argentina’s sovereignty claim over the Falkland Islands. Instead, the self-styled libertarian merely referred to Trump’s words last Monday. Asked at the White House whether he was reviewing the US position on the islands, the US president had said: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.” The far-right president then portrayed Trump’s response as a “threat” that was “not innocuous”. “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” he said. View image in fullscreen Stanley, the capital of the Falkland Islands. In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of the islanders voted to remain a British overseas territory. Photograph: Rob Carter/Alamy The US has formally recognised the UK’s de facto administration of the islands but has not taken a formal position on sovereignty. The first reports of a possible revision emerged in April, when an internal Pentagon email reported by Reuters raised the prospect of Washington reconsidering its stance as one possible way of punishing Nato allies that declined to join the Iran war. In Thursday’s interview, Trump said of the UK: “Your country was not there to help me. We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader [Keir Starmer], ‘why don’t you send a couple of ships?’. He said, ‘We don’t have any’. It was pretty sad, the whole thing.” Despite the expectations created by Milei and his supporters – the president summoned all his ministers to stand alongside him – the main new elements of the speech were a few decrees announced by the president. One of them was to speed up sanctions “against those participating in oil extraction initiatives”, specifically citing an offshore oil project in the North Falkland Basin led by the Israeli company Navitas alongside its British partner Rockhopper. Milei claimed the project violated a UN call for neither Argentina nor the UK to take unilateral action in the territory. Read more Despite his “radical” austerity policies, Milei also said he would sign an emergency decree to increase resources for the defence ministry, prioritising the construction of an integrated naval base in Tierra del Fuego. The project to build a base there predates Milei, and construction began in 2022. The UK said earlier this week that its position on the Falklands was “longstanding and unwavering”. It said in a statement: “Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders’ right to self-determination is paramount. The UK’s position is clear. The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory.” Some analysts had already viewed Milei’s recent embrace of the Malvinas cause as another attempt to create a “smokescreen” at the lowest point of his popularity since taking office. He is expected to seek re-election next year. Amid corruption allegations involving members of his government and poor economic results – his “chainsaw” austerity policies have brought inflation under control, but unemployment and poverty have risen – the far-right president has increasingly turned up the volume on controversial measures, including claims of an anti-Argentina campaign dating back to the World Cup, attacks on Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and an immigration crackdown modelled on the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Many have also noted that his interest in the issue is recent. Milei had long described himself as a great admirer of Margaret Thatcher, the British prime minister during the 1982 Falklands war, and only began adopting a public pro-sovereignty stance a few months ago, after reports emerged that the US might be reconsidering its position. The far-right leader also dismissed the principle of self-determination invoked by the UK – in a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of the islanders voted to remain a British overseas territory. Echoing the same phrase used by Argentina’s national team on a banner celebrating their victory over England in the World Cup semi-final, Milei said that “The Malvinas are Argentinian.” Explore more on these topics Argentina Javier Milei Falkland Islands Americas news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story UK hits back at Argentinian Falklands claim and insists islands remain British White House backs Argentina players over Falklands banner in World Cup semi-final ‘Malvinas are Argentinian’: World Cup holders celebrate win over England with Falklands banner Could Trump withdraw US support for UK sovereignty of Falklands? Photograph: Angelina Katsanis/AP ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) Appeals court rejects Democrat LaMonica McIver’s bid to toss charges over ICE protest New Jersey congresswoman, charged with interfering with immigration arrest, set to face trial over May 2025 incident José Olivares Thu 19 Nov 2026 16.57 EST Last modified on Thu 19 Nov 2026 18.32 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An appeals court decided on Thursday that the Democratic New Jersey representative LaMonica McIver will continue to face charges related to a skirmish outside an immigration detention center last year when she attempted to conduct an oversight visit there. The court’s decision to decline McIver’s request to overturn the court’s earlier ruling comes just a day after she pressed the homeland security secretary for the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement operations, telling the secretary: “You are killing people.” Now, with the court’s decision, she is facing a likely trial for the May 2025 incident. ICE offers contractor operating deportation flights windfall and secrecy, data shows Read more “Because of a weaponized Department of Justice, and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in a statement on Thursday. “Now, due to the disappointing decision by the third circuit, we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.” McIver was charged last year with assaulting, resisting, impeding and interfering with federal officers. The prosecution led to a lengthy legal battle, with McIver claiming the prosecution represented a political attack by the Trump administration. McIver has attempted to have the case dismissed on various grounds, including by arguing the constitution protects her from prosecution. The third circuit court of appeals rejected her arguments in August and on Thursday declined her request to have an “en banc” hearing, meaning the full bench of active judges refused to reconsider the three-judge panel’s decision. “This result is frustrating, but my lawyers and I are looking at every possible option for what comes next,” McIver added. The case stems from a heated oversight visit to a contentious immigration detention center in her state. Last May, McIver arrived at the Delaney Hall detention center, a large Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in New Jersey , for a congressional oversight visit. She arrived with two other members of Congress and Newark’s mayor, Ras Baraka. McIver and the other officials were barred access into the detention center. While standing outside Delaney Hall, a federal agent attempted to arrest Baraka for refusing to depart the premises. According to a homeland security agent’s declaration , McIver intervened, attempting to prevent Baraka from being arrested. Federal officials claim that during the pandemonium, McIver “slammed her forearm” into the homeland security agent and “forcibly” struck another deportation officer with her forearms. “I hope that everyone who feels that way will stand with me in my fight against these unjust charges, because while I am the first lawmaker they have tried to jail, I will surely not be the last,” McIver said. The court’s decision came a day after McIver got into a heated exchange with the homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, for leading the agencies in charge of the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The Delaney Hall facility has fallen under repeated scrutiny since it began detaining immigrants arrested by ICE again in 2025. At least three people detained at Delaney Hall have died. And the facility was the site of major clashes with ICE earlier this year during protests outside the facility in support of a hunger strike by detained immigrants. McIver brought up conditions inside Delaney Hall and the number of who have died in ICE custody during Wednesday’s House committee hearing with Mullin. “As you know, I am facing 17 years in prison, from this Trump administration, for my work at Delaney,” McIver said on Wednesday, then asked Mullin: “Do you even understand why I have been sounding the alarm about Delaney for so long?” Mullin quipped that he had visited Delaney and said the facility was in “very good condition”. McIver challenged Mullin’s claims, telling him: “History is going to judge you for what you are doing.” “You are killing people. You are killing people,” McIver added during the exchange with Mullin, who told her those claims were false. McIver is the only elected representative facing charges for last year’s Delaney Hall scuffle. The charges against Baraka were dropped.
